explanations.answer: To hold a feast to Him in the wilderness
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Moses, Israel's leader, and his brother Aaron tell Pharaoh, king of Egypt, “Let My people go, so that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness.” (Exodus 5:1) A feast is a gathering, and this one is for the LORD. I love a good gathering, so this message has my vote.

explanations.answer: To go back to their own land for good
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd think so, but this message says nothing about a permanent move. Moses and Aaron say, “Let My people go, so that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness.” (Exodus 5:1) The request is about a feast, and the wilderness is where it happens.

explanations.answer: To rest from their labor for a season
explanations.explanation: Rest sounds nice, I'll give you that. But the message from the LORD doesn't mention rest at all. It says, “Let My people go, so that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness.” (Exodus 5:1) The reason given is a feast to Him.

explanations.answer: Who is the LORD that I should obey Him
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Pharaoh answers, “Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice and let Israel go?” (Exodus 5:2) He doesn't ask about travel plans or schedules. He goes straight at who the LORD is, and he says he doesn't know Him.

explanations.answer: Where will your people go after the feast
explanations.explanation: Good practical question, but Pharaoh never asks it. His question in Exodus 5:2 is “Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice and let Israel go?” He's not planning the trip. He's questioning the One who sent the message.

explanations.answer: How many of your people want to leave
explanations.explanation: Pharaoh isn't counting heads here. He asks, “Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice and let Israel go?” (Exodus 5:2) The question is about the LORD, not about a headcount. He does bring up numbers a little later, but not as a question.

True, friend. Moses and Aaron ask to go on a three-day journey to sacrifice to the LORD, “or He may strike us with plagues or with the sword.” (Exodus 5:3) They say it right to the king's face. That takes nerve, and I'd have been hiding behind my own mustache.

It's actually true. Moses and Aaron say, “Please let us go on a three-day journey into the wilderness to sacrifice to the LORD our God, or He may strike us with plagues or with the sword.” (Exodus 5:3) The warning is right there in the verse, so don't let the plain wording fool you.

explanations.answer: Moses and Aaron would stop a lot of workers
explanations.explanation: Exactly, baker. Pharaoh says, “Look, the people of the land are now numerous, and you would be stopping them from their labor.” (Exodus 5:5) His point is about the work getting held up. A big crew means a big pause.

explanations.answer: There are too many people to travel that far
explanations.explanation: Pharaoh never says the trip is too far for them. He says, “Look, the people of the land are now numerous, and you would be stopping them from their labor.” (Exodus 5:5) His worry is the work that would stop, not the distance.

explanations.answer: They could grow strong enough to fight Egypt
explanations.explanation: That's a dramatic theory, but the text doesn't give it. Pharaoh says, “Look, the people of the land are now numerous, and you would be stopping them from their labor.” (Exodus 5:5) The concern he names is the labor, and fighting never comes up.

Straw is it. Pharaoh says, “You shall no longer supply the people with straw for making bricks.” (Exodus 5:7) Straw is one small ingredient, and he takes that away without lowering anything else. Little things matter when you're making a whole pile of bricks.
Mortar is a good brick-world word, but it isn't in this verse. Pharaoh says, “You shall no longer supply the people with straw for making bricks.” (Exodus 5:7) Straw is the one thing he cuts off.

Clay sounds right for bricks, I'll give you that. But verse 7 only names one thing being taken away. Pharaoh says, “You shall no longer supply the people with straw for making bricks.” (Exodus 5:7) It's the straw.

Reasonable guess, friend, but it's the other way around. Pharaoh says, “But require of them the same quota of bricks as before; do not reduce it.” (Exodus 5:8) The straw is gone, and the number stays exactly where it was. That's the whole sting of this order.

False is right. Pharaoh tells the taskmasters, “But require of them the same quota of bricks as before; do not reduce it.” (Exodus 5:8) The people lose the straw supply, but the number of bricks stays the same. Less help, same load.

Lazy is the word. Pharaoh says, “For they are lazy; that is why they are crying out, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’” (Exodus 5:8) That's what Pharaoh calls them. Notice he's the one saying it, and he's the one handing out the orders.
Afraid is a natural guess, but Pharaoh doesn't use it. He says, “For they are lazy; that is why they are crying out, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’” (Exodus 5:8) His word for them is lazy.

Hungry makes sense as a guess, but it's not what Pharaoh says. He tells the taskmasters, “For they are lazy; that is why they are crying out, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’” (Exodus 5:8) Lazy is the word he picks.

True, baker. Pharaoh says, “Make the work harder on the men so they will be occupied and pay no attention to these lies.” (Exodus 5:9) Lies is his word for the message from Moses and Aaron. He thinks busy hands will keep minds from wandering.

It's actually true. Pharaoh says, “Make the work harder on the men so they will be occupied and pay no attention to these lies.” (Exodus 5:9) He wants them occupied and not listening. The text says it plainly.

explanations.answer: All over the land of Egypt
explanations.explanation: That's right. “So the people scattered all over the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.” (Exodus 5:12) Scattered is a good word for it. Picture a whole workforce trying to find the same thing in every direction.

explanations.answer: Only to the fields of Goshen
explanations.explanation: The verse is bigger than one spot. It says, “So the people scattered all over the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.” (Exodus 5:12) Nothing there narrows it to one place. They had to spread out wide.

The wilderness is where Moses and Aaron asked to go for the feast, but the straw hunt happens somewhere else. “So the people scattered all over the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.” (Exodus 5:12) They stay in Egypt, working. Same work, bigger search.

True, friend, and this part is heavy. The Israelite foremen were beaten and asked, “Why have you not fulfilled your quota of bricks yesterday or today, as you did before?” (Exodus 5:14) They were put over the people by Pharaoh's taskmasters, so they felt it first. I think this one hurts.

It's true, and it's a heavy verse. The foremen were beaten and asked, “Why have you not fulfilled your quota of bricks yesterday or today, as you did before?” (Exodus 5:14) The question is right there in the text. I think this is one of the hard parts of the story.

People is it. The foremen say, “Look, your servants are being beaten, but the fault is with your own people.” (Exodus 5:16) They are speaking to Pharaoh, the one they call king. They say it right to his face, and that's brave.

Gods doesn't show up in that sentence. The foremen say, “Look, your servants are being beaten, but the fault is with your own people.” (Exodus 5:16) Their words are about Pharaoh's people, not his gods.
Heart sounds poetic, but the foremen don't say it. They tell Pharaoh, “Look, your servants are being beaten, but the fault is with your own people.” (Exodus 5:16) The word is people.

I wish that were the story, friend, but no. Pharaoh says, “You will be given no straw, yet you must deliver the full quota of bricks.” (Exodus 5:18) The straw stays gone, and the number stays full. No deal, no discount.

False is right. Pharaoh tells the foremen, “Now get to work. You will be given no straw, yet you must deliver the full quota of bricks.” (Exodus 5:18) There's no bargain here. He repeats the order and sends them back.

explanations.answer: May the LORD look on you and judge you
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The foremen say, “May the LORD look upon you and judge you.” (Exodus 5:21) They say it to Moses and Aaron, who were standing there waiting for them. That's a tough greeting after the day they've had.

explanations.answer: May the LORD bless you for your courage
explanations.explanation: I wish they'd said that, but it's not the text. The foremen say, “May the LORD look upon you and judge you.” (Exodus 5:21) They're upset, and their words show it.

explanations.answer: May the LORD go with you to Pharaoh
explanations.explanation: Moses and Aaron have already been to Pharaoh, so that's not what the foremen say. Their words are, “May the LORD look upon you and judge you.” (Exodus 5:21) They are not in a sending-off mood.
True, and it's a heavy one. The foremen say, “you have placed in their hand a sword to kill us!” (Exodus 5:21) Their is Pharaoh and his officials. I think they're scared, and the words sound like it.

It's true, and it's a heavy line. The foremen tell Moses and Aaron, “you have made us a stench before Pharaoh and his officials; you have placed in their hand a sword to kill us!” (Exodus 5:21) The sword part is right there in the verse. I think they're frightened.

explanations.answer: Why have You brought trouble upon this people
explanations.explanation: That's right. Moses asks, “Lord, why have You brought trouble upon this people?” (Exodus 5:22) He takes the question straight to the LORD instead of keeping it to himself. When something doesn't make sense, that's a good place to bring it.

explanations.answer: Who will You send to Pharaoh instead of me
explanations.explanation: Moses never asks to be replaced here. He asks, “Lord, why have You brought trouble upon this people? Is this why You sent me?” (Exodus 5:22) He's asking why, not who else.

explanations.answer: How long must Your people wait in Egypt
explanations.explanation: That's a fair question, but it's not the one Moses asks. He says, “Lord, why have You brought trouble upon this people?” (Exodus 5:22) The word that matters here is why.

True, baker. Right after asking why, Moses adds, “Is this why You sent me?” (Exodus 5:22) That's an honest question, and he says it to the LORD Himself. I think he's trying to make sense of a hard day.
It's true. Moses asks the LORD, “Lord, why have You brought trouble upon this people? Is this why You sent me?” (Exodus 5:22) The second question is right there in the same verse.
Delivered is the word. Moses says, “and You have not delivered Your people in any way.” (Exodus 5:23) He says it in the LORD's presence. That's Moses being honest about how things look to him.
Tested makes a sensible guess, but it's not the word in the verse. Moses says, “and You have not delivered Your people in any way.” (Exodus 5:23) Delivered is what he's talking about.
Punished doesn't appear here. Moses says, “and You have not delivered Your people in any way.” (Exodus 5:23) The word he uses is delivered.

explanations.answer: What the LORD will do to Pharaoh
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The LORD says, “Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh…” (Exodus 6:1) Moses brought a hard question, and the LORD answers by pointing to what He will do. The answer is the LORD's own action.

explanations.answer: A new leader rise up in Egypt
explanations.explanation: The LORD doesn't mention a new leader. He says, “Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh…” (Exodus 6:1) What Moses will see is something the LORD does.
Elders don't come up in this verse. The LORD tells Moses, “Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh…” (Exodus 6:1) The focus is on what He does, not on anyone else turning.

explanations.answer: Drive them out of his land
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD says, “…because of My strong hand he will drive them out of his land.” (Exodus 6:1) Pharaoh was saying no a few verses ago, and now the LORD says he will drive them out. That is a big turn.
The verse doesn't picture Pharaoh leading the way. The LORD says, “…because of My strong hand he will drive them out of his land.” (Exodus 6:1) The word is drive.
Nothing in the verse says secret. The LORD says, “…because of My strong hand he will drive them out of his land.” (Exodus 6:1) Drive is the word He uses.
